about.title: Commerce Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Commerce sits at a logistics crossroads, with warehousing, trucking, and manufacturing jobs clustered near the I-5 corridor and Telegraph Road. Workers in these industries face real risks — forklift accidents, falls from loading docks, repetitive strain, and equipment malfunctions among them. In California, workers' compensation is generally the only path against your employer, regardless of who caused the accident. But that's not always the full picture. If a subcontractor, property owner, delivery driver, or equipment manufacturer contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim against that third party. Sorting out which path applies — and whether both apply — takes a careful look at the facts. We handle workplace injury claims in Commerce and can evaluate the details, explain your options in plain terms, and help you move forward without added stress on top of recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Injured Workers in Commerce Choose Us

items.title: We Help Untangle Comp vs. Third-Party Claims
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker can open a separate claim. We can help identify which applies to your case.

items.title: We Understand the Reporting Clock
items.desc: California law generally requires reporting a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days. Missing that window can complicate your claim, so timing matters from day one.

items.title: We Know Retaliation Is Illegal
items.desc: Employers cannot legally punish you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If you're worried about your job, we can explain your protections before you make any decisions.

items.question: I work in a Commerce warehouse near I-5 — can I still sue my employer if I'm hurt on the job?
items.answer: In most cases, workers' compensation is your exclusive remedy against your employer, even if the accident wasn't entirely your fault. However, if a third party — like a delivery contractor, property owner, or equipment manufacturer — contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim against them. We can review your specific situation to see if a third-party claim applies.

items.question: How long do I have to report a workplace injury in California?
items.answer: You generally need to report the injury to your employer within 30 days. Waiting too long can create problems with your workers' comp claim, so it's best to report as soon as possible after the injury happens.

items.question: What if I'm afraid my employer will retaliate if I file a claim?
items.answer: Retaliation for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim is illegal under California law. If you're facing pressure or fear repercussions, we can walk you through your protections and help you understand your next steps.
